reviewDecision.reason: Two blocking issues, both the same root cause: the deprecated-workload exemption was implemented at the admission layer only. ValidateCreate kept the whole-object check so an exempt RoleBasedGroupSet can never scale up or heal, and the RBAC/watches are still removed unconditionally so an admitted group still cannot be reconciled. Both contradict a sentence this PR adds to the chart README. Mitigating factor stated in the review: the default is now true, so nothing reaches an operator who does not opt in.

corrections.withdrawn: The scale-up half. Refusing to CREATE a child RBG with a deprecated template is AS DESIGNED: the README already lists "creating a RoleBasedGroup/RoleBasedGroupSet whose roles use a deprecated workload type" as rejected, and a controller-created child falls under that. If scale-up kept working the toggle would have no teeth. The original comment framed a deliberate decision as a defect.

retained.detail: The rejected-list does not mention RBGSet scaling, and two lines above it the same paragraph says an existing group "stays writable (and scalable)" -- for RBGSet those contradict, since its scaling IS child creation. One of the two must change.

RoleBasedGroupSetValidator.ValidateUpdate does not look at spec.replicas, so `replicas: 2 -> 4` is admitted and persisted and the controller then retries a denied create forever; spec/status diverge permanently with no condition or event. If scale-up is meant to be refused, refusing a replica increase at admission is the same decision enforced where the user finds out.

With replicas=2 and index 1 lost to node failure / GC / kubectl delete, the controller's attempt to refill it is rejected, so capacity goes 2 -> 1 permanently. Verified directly: the object built to refill the missing index is refused by ValidateCreate. Distinct from scale-up -- this is an existing workload degrading at a moment the operator did not choose.

corrections.lesson: Packaged a design decision and a real defect under one blocker heading ("can never scale up or heal"). The two halves needed separating before publishing, not after.
